abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Numerous studies have investigated the biological activities of honey, emphasizing its antimicrobial, antioxidant, and therapeutic properties. However, a comprehensive examination of the bacteria isolated from honey has been largely overlooked. This study aimed to bridge that gap by exploring the relationship between the bioactivities of honey and the bacterial spores it contains. Furthermore, there is no comparison between the polysaccharides in honey such as levan and its inherent bacteria. Accordingly, various enzymes, including levansucrase, invertase, glucose oxidase, amylase, and catalase, were assessed in Nigerian mountain honey and their inherent seven bacterial isolates. Honey and its isolates showed levansucrase production to various degrees where the highest activity was obtained with isolate NO.4 and the honey recorded (21U/ml). Additionally, honey and its isolates showed varied activities between (171–465 U/ml), (88–250 U/ml) for amylase and glucose oxidase respectively. The highest catalase activity was recorded by isolate No 4 based on the qualitative test. Interestingly, all isolates lacked protease activity. Honey and specific isolates inhibited various pathogenic bacteria, including Salmonella enterica Typhi, Escherichia coli, and Bacillus cereus. Also, fungi such as Candida albicans. In addition, honey and its isolates had high antioxidant activities ranging from 58 to 77%. The polysaccharides Lev1, Lev2, and honey have no cytotoxic effects on normal cells. They were identified as levans based on FTIR and NMR. Honey and lev1, lev2 showed cytotoxicity against HCT116 cell lines (61.5, 59.5, and 53.70%), respectively. Interestingly, the study found a strong link between the biological activities of the bacteria and the honey itself.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Consuming honey is linked to several health benefits, according to many researches. Bees from different species make honey, a naturally sweet material, from the secretions or nectar of plants. Around 80 % of honey's composition is made up of simple and complex sugars, including fructose and glucose, as well as at least 22 additional sugars. It also contains potentially active ingredients such flavonoids, phenolics, vitamins, enzymes, minerals, and amino acids.1 The following enzymes can be found in honey: proteases, α-amylase, α-glucosidase, β-glucosidase, invertase, glucose oxidase, catalase, and glucosylceramidase.2 Snowdon and Cliver3 mentioned honey as a diverse microbiome, with most of its constituents coming from pollen, flowers, soil, air, dust, and the digestive system of honeybees. Furthermore, human handling of honey may add some secondary microbial pollutants. Honey contains various microorganisms, including bacteria, yeasts, and molds.

Most microorganisms, including bacteria, cannot grow or procreate in honey; that is, they are inactive (dormant), and this is due to the osmophilic nature of honey. Honey was known as a reservoir of probiotic bacteria which take part in different bioactivities. The honey microbiome has drawn attention and many studied talks in the honey as novel source for levansucrase which form the levan polymer.4, 5, 6 While honey's bioactivities are widely recognized, there is limited understanding of how the endospores in honey (which could survive harsh conditions) contribute to these effects. Further studies are required to explore this potential connection and until this moment, there is little data regarding whether the bioactivities of honeys correlated with their endospore and there is scarce evidence about the job of bacterial honey in honey function. Hernandez et al7 talks about the role of honey in alteration and regulation of the gut microbiota which would lead to health benefits, but he does not consider the interference of the honey microbiota with the gut intestinal. The study by Hamdy et al8 likely discusses how bacteria isolated from honey may contain levan polymers, which could contribute to its prebiotic potential. Specifically, bacterial honey may serve as a natural source of levan, which could enhance the honey's ability to support beneficial gut microbiota. This prebiotic activity could be one of the mechanisms through which bacterial honey exerts health benefits, beyond its traditional antibacterial and antioxidant properties. The connection between honey and the bacterial isolates that produce biopolymers like levan and dextran lies in the symbiotic relationship between honey and the microorganisms that naturally inhabit it. Honey, a complex and bioactive substance, provides an environment where bacteria can thrive, and in turn, these bacteria may produce valuable biopolymers that contribute to both the honey’s properties and human health.9, 10

While there have been rare studies on enzymes found in honey such as amylase, invertase, glucose oxidase and catalase11 there is a relative lack of comprehensive research on enzymes produced by bacterial honey, particularly in the context of honey or related products.

In a rare study, some researchers paid attention for the enzymes produced from the honey isolates. For instance, amylase was found in the honey samples from which different isolates of amylolytic-active bacteria were obtained.12, 13 Dextranase produced from the bacterial honey isolate Bacillus subtilis was reported by Esawy et al.14 Osés et al15 reported that increased levels of glucose oxidase in honey are associated with higher hydrogen peroxide production and lower catalase activity. Since glucose oxidase is of bee origin and bees tightly regulate the ripening process of honey, it can be expected that most honeys globally contain relatively consistent levels of this enzyme.

There is urgent demand for new antibiotics to share in solving the antimicrobial resistant problem Since the discovery of antibiotics, infections resistant to several treatments have quickly emerged due to the overuse and under consumption of these medications. Gram-positive bacteria, like Staphylococcus aureus, and Gram-negative bacteria, like Escherichia coli, are particularly notable for their propensity to develop multiple mechanisms of resistance to antibiotics, posing a threat to global public health.15 There have been suggestions that honey's microbes may be a source of new antibacterial drugs.16 Much research focused on the antioxidant activity of bacteria to lower the danger of ROS generation through food consumption. This reduces the oxidative damage to cells, which is crucial in the development of cancer. Hamdy et al5 mentioned the antioxidant activities of different bacteria isolated from honey. One of the three most common malignant tumors in the world is colorectal cancer (CRC). Currently, surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy are the main suggested therapies for it; however, all of them come with a significant recurrence rate and a poor prognosis17.Researchers are concentrating on looking for extremely effective and non-toxic natural medications to control tumor microenvironment (TME), trigger cell apoptosis, and limit cell proliferation and spread.18 Many studies mentioned levan as an anticancer agent and protective agent against chemotherapy.19, 20, 21

In this research seven bacterial were isolated from mountain Nigerian honey and comprehensive study to evaluate the bioactivities of the honey and their isolates. The results showed that the honey and their isolates produced levansucrase, amylase, invertase, glucose oxidase and catalase activity with various degrees. The protease was absent completely from the mountain honey and their isolates. Also, the honey and its isolates are characterized by strong antimicrobial and antioxidant activities. All the isolates were polysaccharides producer which identified as levan. Based on the lack of cytotoxicity on normal cells, two levans were chosen to assess HCT116 (Colon cell line) and A431 (skin cancer) cytotoxicity.

sec.title: Isolation of bacteria from Nigerian honey
sec.p: Nigerian honey was collected at the mature stage; serial dilutions were made for the honey sample (10–9). Then it was spread on nutrient agar (NG) and incubated at 37 °C for 24 h Seven types of colonies were obtained. One colony of each bacterium was picked and purified by serial subculture and plating For long-term preservation, the isolates were maintained in Bendolph tubes containing 1 mL of nutrient broth supplemented with a drop of glycerol and then stored at −80 °C.

sec.title: Morphological characteristics of the isolated bacteria
sec.p: Once the isolate's slide culture was stained with Gram stain using the Biodiagnostic Bacterial Strains kit (Batch: 180219), it was inspected under a light microscope at a 400X magnification

sec.title: 16S rDNA-Based Molecular Identification
sec.p: Genomic DNA was extracted from bacterial isolates cultured in LB broth (24 h) using the Gene JET Genomic DNA Purification Kit (Thermo Scientific, Lithuania), following centrifugation and washing with 0.85 % NaCl.22 The 16S rRNA gene was amplified using universal primers 8F and 1492R in a 50 μL PCR reaction containing DreamTaq Green Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), under the following conditions: 95 °C for 4 min;35 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s; 50 °C for 45 s; 72 °C for 1 min; and a final extension at 72 °C for 10 min.23 PCR products were separated by agarose gel electrophoresis (1X TBE buffer, ethidium bromide), and bands were purified using the Wizard Genomic DNA Purification Kit (Promega, USA) Sequencing was conducted by Macrogen (Korea), and sequence analysis was performed using FinchTV v140, BLASTn (NCBI) for homology search, ClustalW v21 for multiple alignment and MEGA X for phylogenetic tree construction using the neighbor-joining method of Kumar et al.24

sec.title: Production medium and levansucrase assay
sec.p: The production medium contained (g/l): Surcose (80), K2HPO4 (3), MgSO4 (02) and yeast extract (2) The medium was centrifuge to separate the cells from the culture filtrate (CF). The reaction consisted of 1 ml acetate buffer (0.2 M) at pH 5.2, 1 ml dist water, 1 ml culture filtrate (CF), and 2 ml sucrose (20 %). The incubation was done at 40 °C for 15 min. The levansucrase assay was carried out using the methodology described by Yanase et al.25 The amount of enzyme that produced decreasing sugars equal to one mol of glucose per minute was defined as one unit of enzyme activity.

sec.title: Production medium (g/L) and amylase activity
sec.p: The production medium contained (g/l): Potato starch (10), peptone (5), yeast extract (3), FeSO4 (0.2), NaCl (1). Two mL of 1 % starch in 0.1 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 5.2) and one mL of CF made up the reaction mixture and were incubated at 40 °C for 15 min. The enzyme assay was determined using Miller's dinitrosalicylic acid (DNS) technique.26 The dinitrosalicylic acid (DNS) method is a technique for estimating the concentration of reducing sugars in a sample. At 540 nm, the resultant color was measured Under test conditions, the quantity of enzyme that releases one mole of glucose per minute is known as one unit (U) of enzyme activity.

sec.title: Production medium (g/L) and alkaline protease activity
sec.p: The production medium contained (g/L): alkali-soluble casein (20), glucose (10), K2HPO4 (1.5), and Na2HPO4 (1.5). Alkaline protease activity was determined using casein as the substrate, according to the method of Gessesse and Gashe27 with slight modifications. The reaction mixture, with a total volume of (1.7 mL), consisted of 1.5 mL of 1 % casein solution prepared in 50 mM glycine–NaOH buffer (pH 8.0) and 0.2 mL of crude filtrate (CF) as the enzyme source. After incubation at 37 °C for 20 min, the reaction was terminated by adding 2 mL of 10 % trichloroacetic acid (TCA), followed by centrifugation. A blank was prepared by adding TCA before the enzyme solution. To 0.5 mL of the resulting supernatant, 2.5 mL of 0.5 M sodium carbonate and 0.5 mL of 2 N Folin–Ciocalteu phenol reagent (diluted 1:3 with distilled water) were added. The mixture was incubated at room temperature for 30 min, and the absorbance was measured at 660 nm.
One unit of protease activity was defined as the amount of enzyme that releases 1 µmol of tyrosine per minute under the assay conditions.

sec.title: Production medium (g/L) and invertase activity
sec.p: The production medium contained (g/L): sucrose (20), yeast extract (1), MgSO4 (0.2), K2HPO4 (0.5), and agar (25), with the pH adjusted to 6.0. According to Miller,25 the release of reducing sugars is a reliable indicator of invertase activity. The reaction mixture consisted of 0.5 mL of 1 % sucrose (substrate) and 0.5 mL of crude filtrate (CF), incubated at 40 °C for 15 min. The reaction was terminated by adding 1 mL of dinitrosalicylic acid (DNS) reagent, followed by heating for 5 min to allow full color development. Absorbance was measured at 540 nm. One unit (U) of invertase activity was defined as the amount of enzyme that releases 1 µmole of reducing sugars per minute under the assay conditions.

sec.title: Production medium (g/L) and glucose oxidase activity
sec.p: The production medium contained (g/L): glucose (50), sucrose (2), MgSO4 (0.2), K2HPO4 (0.5), yeast extract (10), and NaCl (0.05).

Glucose oxidase activity was assayed using the following reaction mixture: 100 µL of crude filtrate (CF), 2 mL of 1 M glucose, 1 mL of 0.1 % benzoquinone, and 900 µL of 0.1 M citrate–phosphate buffer (pH 5.0). The reaction mixture was incubated at 27 °C for 10 min, and absorbance was measured at 290 nm to determine enzyme activity.

sec.title: Antimicrobial activity of honey and its bacterial isolates
sec.p: Using cell −free culture supernatants (CFCS) of the isolated strains against pathogenic bacteria, such as Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 29213, Bacillus cereus ATC33018, Salmonella enterica Typhi28ATCC 14028, and Escherichia coli MC1400 Candida albicans NRRL Y-477 was used as an example of fungi.

The antimicrobial activity of the isolates was assessed using the agar well diffusion method.29 A 5 mm diameter well was created, filled with 100 μL of CFCS from each honey isolate, and appropriately labeled with the isolates' names. The honey sample was diluted 1:10 (sterilized H2O) and 100 μL was used to evaluate the antimicrobial activity Following two hours at room temperature, the plates were incubated for twenty-four hours at 37 °C. The zone diameter of inhibition (ZDI) was estimated in cm. The data were provided as mean ± SD, and the experiments were run in triplicate.

sec.title: Antioxidant activity of honey and honey isolates
sec.p: The reaction mixture was incubated at 37 °C for 100 min and scavenged DPPH was observed by measuring the decrease in OD at 517 nm Ascorbic acid was used as a standard drug, and the scavenging activity of bacterial strains was determined using the following formula (%) = [1 − sample (OD)/blank (OD)] × 100.30

sec.title: Polysaccharides precipitation
sec.p: As previously mentioned, the polysaccharide-producing bacterial isolates were grown on a specified substrate-levan production medium. Following growth, the culture filtrate was centrifuged to get rid of the bacteria cells, and then two volumes of absolute ethanol were used to precipitate the levan compounds.

sec.title: Cytotoxicity and anticancer activity
sec.p: Cell viability was assessed using the method of Mosmann,31 which measures mitochondrial-dependent reduction of yellow 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) to purple formazan. Three cell lines were evaluated: human pancreatic colon cancer (HCT-116, CCL-247; ATCC), skin cancer (A-431, CRL-1555; ATCC), and normal retinal pigment epithelial cells (hTERT RPE-1, ATCC).

Cells were suspended at a concentration of 1 × 104 cells/well in DMEM/F-12 medium supplemented with 1 % antibiotic–antimycotic solution (10,000 U/mL penicillin, 10,000 µg/mL streptomycin, and 25 µg/mL amphotericin B) and 1 % L-glutamine. The cell suspension was seeded into 96-well microtiter plates and incubated at 37 °C in a humidified 5 % CO2 atmosphere for 24 h.
Levan was dissolved in distilled water to a final concentration of 100 µg/mL immediately prior to treatment.

sec.title: Separation of levan and thin-layer chromatography (TLC)
sec.p: The levan producing organisms were cultivated on a BM as described above. After growth, the culture was centrifuged to remove bacterial cells; then the levan was precipitated with two volumes of absolute ethanol. The precipitate was collected and dried under vacuum. To do plates, two ascents of acetonitrile and water (85:15, v/v) were implemented. To see the carbohydrates on TLC plates, the plates were dipped in sulfuric acid (5 %, v/v) in ethanol containing 0.5 % (w/v) of naphthol. The plates were then heated on a hot plate at 110 °C for 10 min.32

sec.title: Fourier transform infrared (FTIR)
sec.p: In summary, FTIR spectrophotometry (Agilent Cary 630) was used to identify the functional groups in the purified levan preparations over a wavenumber of [4000–400] cm−1. Accordingly, 10 mg of each lyophilized levan was combined with 200 mg of potassium bromide (KBr), and the mixture was then pressed to form a 1 mm thick mold.

sec.title: 1H and 13C NMR analysis
sec.p: Levan structure was elucidated using the analysis of 1H and 13C NMR spectra. Levan and inulin samples were dissolved in distilled H2O and the measurements performed using a JEOL-GX-500 NMR spectrophotometer.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Data evaluation was conducted using Microsoft Excel (2007). All data is displayed as the mean ± standard error of the means. The average of the repeated measurements provided the value for each replicate.

sec.title: Bacterial isolation and description
sec.p: Seven bacterial strains were successfully isolated from Nigerian mountain honey and characterized using light microscopy and morphological assessment. The isolates exhibited rod-shaped morphology and were gram-positive. Except for isolate 2, all colonies appeared smooth and mucoid in texture (Table 1). Identification of the bacterial strains was carried out through 16S rRNA gene sequencing, which revealed that the isolates belonged to the genus Bacillus. Specifically, they were identified as Bacillus paramycoides, Bacillus albus, Bacillus pumilus, Bacillus spizizenii, Bacillus tequilensis, and Bacillus velezensis. The 16S rRNA sequences of all isolates showed a high degree of similarity (≥96 %) to reference Bacillus species available in the NCBI database, confirming their taxonomic classification (Table 2).

sec.title: Evaluation of different enzymes production by the honey bacterial isolates
Levansucrase
sec.p: To varying degrees, the seven honey isolates were judged to be good levansucrase and levan producers (Fig. 1). Furthermore, the findings (Fig. 1) demonstrated that honey was an excellent source of levansucrase on its own. The maximum enzyme production was found in isolate NO 4 (198.44 U/ml), followed by isolate NO. 7 (159.33 U/ml).

caption.p: Screening for levansucrase production by the seven honey isolates.

sec.title: Amylase
sec.p: According to the results, amylase was detected in raw honey and recorded (171.00 U/ml). On the other hand, all the isolates showed different amylase activity in different quantities. The highest amylase activity was produced by isolates NO.2, NO.3 and NO.4 in the presence of potato starch (465, 455.00, and 449.00 U/ml) respectively (Fig. 2).

caption.p: Screening for amylase production by the seven honey isolates.

sec.title: Invertase
sec.p: Consequently, the invertase production of the seven honey isolates and Nigerian mountain honey varied. Out of all the bacterial isolates, mountain honey had the highest invertase activity (115.00 U/ml) (Fig. 3). The isolate NO.1 recorded the lowest enzyme production (38.35 U/ml), while isolate NO 3 displayed the highest enzyme production (91.53 U/ml).

caption.p: Screening for invertase production by the seven honey isolates.

sec.title: Glucose oxidase
sec.p: The glucose oxidase production was determined in the honey and their bacterial isolates Isolate No 1 exhibited the highest GOX production (250.67 U/ml), followed by Mountain Honey (233.75 U/ml), followed by isolate NO.4 (200.67 U/ml) as seen in the results (Fig. 4). The other isolates produced between 88.67 and 145.33 U/ml of enzymes. The isolate NO.5 (88.67 U/ml) had the lowest production.

caption.p: Screening for glucose oxidase production by the seven honey isolates.

sec.title: Catalase
sec.p: The catalase production was evaluated in this study. When catalase was measured qualitatively, honey and each strain produced impressive amounts of the enzyme, albeit to varying degrees (Table 3). Furthermore, the findings demonstrated that Mountain Honey and its isolates contained no protease enzyme at all.

caption.p: The qualitative production of catalase by the seven honey bacterial isolates.

sec.title: Antimicrobial activity of Nigerian mountain honey and its isolated bacteria
sec.p: The Nigerian mountain honey showed a promising antibacterial action against all of the studied harmful bacteria, according to the data (Table 4). The seven honey isolates demonstrated observable antifungal action against Candida albicans, as indicated by the results in Table 4. Salmonella enterica Typhi exhibited no antimicrobial susceptibility to isolates No. 3 and 4. However, it showed measurable zones of inhibition ranging from 3.0 to 3.3 cm when treated with honey and isolates NO. 1, 2, 5, 6, and 7. Isolate NO. 7 exhibited the highest antimicrobial activity against Staphylococcus aureus, producing an inhibition zone of 4.8 cm. This was followed by isolates NO. 1 and 4, each showing a 2.5 cm zone of inhibition. Isolates NO. 3 and honey also demonstrated moderate activity with 2.0 cm inhibition zones, while isolates NO. 2 and 6 showed no inhibitory effect. Among the seven tested isolates, isolates NO. 4, 6, and 7 exhibited no antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli. In contrast, isolate No. 1 demonstrated the strongest inhibitory effect, with a zone of inhibition measuring 3.2 cm, followed by isolate No. 2 (3.0 cm) and isolate NO.3 (2.5 cm).

caption.p: The antimicrobial activity of the mountain honey and its isolates against different pathogenic microbes.

sec.title: Antioxidant activity of Nigerian mountain honey and its isolated bacteria
sec.p: Seven bacterial isolates from the Nigerian mountain were tested for antioxidant properties. The outcome (Fig. 5) demonstrated that isolates of honey exhibited strong antioxidant activity, ranging from 57 % to 87 %. The antioxidant activity (87.27, 87.37 %) was highest in the honey and its isolate NO7, which both had the same appearance.

caption.p: The antioxidant activity of the Nigerian mountain honey and its bacterial isolates.

sec.title: Cytotoxicity and anticancer activity of honey and its bacterial levan extracts
sec.p: The normal human epithelial cell line (A431) was used to test the cytotoxicity of the seven levans that were isolated from the bacterially fermented medium and the honey. Table 5 displays the results, which indicate that Lev 1, Lev 2, and raw honey exhibit little cytotoxicity and a high degree of cell survival. To test their anticancer properties against the human tumor cell lines HCT116 (Colon cell line) and A431 (skin cancer), Lev 1, Lev 2, and Nigerian mountain honey were chosen. The outcomes demonstrated that every examined sample had a negative impact on A431 and an anticancer effect on HCT116. For Honey, Lev 1, and Lev 2, the measured cell inhibition values were 61.5, 59.5, and 53.70 %, respectively (Fig. 6).

caption.p: The cytotoxicity of different levans types.
The effect of levan against the human tumor cell line(s): HCT116.

sec.title: TLC
sec.p: Using thin-layer chromatography (TLC), the hydrolysis product of the seven bacterial isolates' polysaccharides was discovered. The findings showed that the primary component of each polymer, fructose, is what makes up lev1 and lev2.

sec.title: FTIR
sec.p:
Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was used to characterize the structure and identify the functional groups of the two purified polymers (Fig. 7). Broad O–H stretching bands were observed at 3259.41 cm−1 (Lev 1) and 3270.72 cm−1 (Lev 2), which are characteristic of hydroxyl groups commonly found in polysaccharides. The broadness of these peaks reflects the presence of extensive hydrogen bonding. C–H stretching vibrations, indicative of methyl groups, were detected at 2933.46 cm−1 (Lev 1) and 2930.03 cm−1 (Lev 2). The absorption peaks at 1642.42 cm−1 and 1643.83 cm−1 correspond to bound water molecules, often retained within polysaccharide matrices. A peak at 1461.61 cm−1 suggests the presence of C

Additional peaks at 1133.16 cm−1, 988.56 cm−1, 1101.84 cm−1, and 1023.93 cm−1 were assigned to C–O–C and C–O stretching vibrations, consistent with glycosidic linkages and ring structures in the polysaccharide backbone.

sec.title: NMR spectrum
sec.p: Fig. 8 displays the 1H and 13C NMR spectra, which highlight the structural complexity and heterogeneity of the exopolysaccharides (EPS) produced by Bacillus subtilis. The 13C NMR spectra revealed six major resonance signals, corresponding to carbon atoms C1–C6 of the sugar units. For Lev 1, signals were observed at δ 61.05, 104.51, 74.84, 77.65, 82.98, and 62.63 ppm, while Lev 2 showed signals at δ 104.66, 61.31, 75.31, 77.10, 80.00, and 63.53 ppm (Fig. 8a & 8c). These chemical shifts are consistent with those typically assigned to the backbone carbons of fructans or levan-type polysaccharides.

caption.p: 1H and 13C NMR data of Lev 1 and Lev 2: (a) 13C NMR of Lev 1, (b) 1H NMR of Lev 1, (c) 13C NMR of Lev 2, and (d) 1H NMR of Lev 2.

sec.p: In the 1H NMR spectra, all proton resonances appeared in the range of δ 3.2–4.0 ppm, indicating the presence of sugar ring protons. A distinct signal near δ 5.0 ppm was also observed, corresponding to the anomeric proton region, supporting the presence of glycosidic linkages (Fig. 8b & 8d).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Honey has been traditionally known for its healing properties, including its ability to combat infections and inflammation.33 Several factors contribute to these bioactivities, and one of them is the interaction with certain bacteria found in honey. However, the potential synergistic or antagonistic effects between honey's bioactivities properties and the bacteria it harbors are still largely uninvestigated. The spore-forming bacteria and yeasts are the main microbes to be concerned about in honey.3, 34 Nonetheless, as new technologies and applications of honey emerge, the need for additional microbiological data on honey will increase.35 In this finding, seven bacterial strains were isolated and purified from Nigerian mountain honey. They were identified based on morphological characterization using a light microscope and 16SRNA. They were gram-positive, endospore-forming, and rod-shaped. Schwarz et al36 reported that the intricate matrix known as the honey microbiota holds ecological data on the pathosphere of the hive, the host microenvironment, and the honeybee hologenome. The Bacillus species identified in all been previously isolated from honey or bee-related sources.37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42 The frequent detection of these microorganisms in honey indicates their ecological adaptation to this environment and underscores their potential utility in antimicrobial and probiotic applications. Previously, Bacillus sp was detected as the most dominant sp in the honey.3 Esawy et al4 mentioned six Bacillus sp from different honey sources with great antiviral activity. Abdelsamad et al6 detected four Bacillus sp isolated from various honey sources They were identified as Bacillus paralicheniformis (2 M), Bacillus subtilis (9A), and Bacillus paranthracis (13 M). Grabek-Lejko et al34 reported that the most commonly isolated honeydew honey species was B pumilus/altitudinis, accounting for 32.96 %, followed by the B cereus group at 20.11 %, and B licheniformis at 13.4 %.

Recent years have seen a surge in interest in levansucrase (EC 2.4.1.10) and its biological synthesis of levan. Many studies have mentioned levansucrase, whether from microorganisms4 or plants.43 At present, honey isolates are identified as new storehouses for levansucrase.4, 7, 9 In this study, seven honey isolates were evaluated as good levansucrase and levan producers to various degrees. Also, the results showed that honey itself was a good source of levansucrase. The presence of this enzyme in honey could represent a key to the interpretation of most of the bioactivities in honey. For instance, the antioxidant activity of levansucrase was mentioned by Salama et al.9 The study suggests the honey benefits not only its constituent but also the synergistic effect between the honey constituent and the products of its microflora, such as the levansucrase. Also, levan, as the main product of levansucrase, was mentioned as a multi-bioactive agent with different functions, such as anticancer44 and antioxidant activities.45 According to our knowledge, no study about the assessment of raw honey for levansucrase detection was mentioned. Traditional medicine has made use of honey products. These products now have more commercial potential due to their historical significance as well as the opportunity to create value from our understanding of the characteristics of their native microbiota.46 Salomón et al47 reported in the honey isolate identified as Bacillus sp and could generate extracellular exopolysaccharides (EPS). Fructose made up most of the carbohydrates in EPS (44.6 %). When Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was used to characterize the structural properties of EPS, it revealed strong similarities to levan.

Previously, honey was known as a good and efficient source of amylase.48 Nagai et al49 reported the purification of two types of alpha-amylases from pure persimmon honey and honeydew. According to our results, amylase was detected in raw honey and recorded 171.00 U/ml. On the other hand, all the isolates showed different amylase activity in different quantities. The highest amylase activity was produced by isolates NO. 2 and 3 in the presence of potato or commercial starch. The obtained amylase activity was higher than Bacillus paramycoides amylase (177.12 U/mg).50 This result could be attributed to the transfer of the amylase gene from honey to the dormant bacteria, which referred to the honey as a new reservoir for potential bacterial amylases. Various amylolytic-active bacterial isolates were isolated from different honey samples.12 Furthermore, amylase derived from honey isolates is expected to be thermostable and resistant to high and low pH, osmolality, and pressure, which have all qualities that are critical for industrial production. This expectation comes from the presence of bacterial isolates in high osmophilic medium. Moreover, the high production amount of amylase from the seven isolates recommended that it play a significant role in the biodegradation of the microbial biofilm, which caused an inevitable risk to humans.51

Invertase is considered one of the most significant hydrolytic enzymes in honey. Oddo et al52 found invertase in 499 honey types. Most researchers agree that bees are the source of invertase in honey.53 As a result, Nigerian mountain honey and its bacterial isolates all had different invertase activities Mountain honey showed the highest invertase activity compared to all bacterial isolates This result introduced a new invertase source to the industrial field, where the invertase was demanded in many sections such as bakery, artificial honey, calf feed, food for honeybees, beverage, confectionary, and others.54

The enzymes glucose oxidase (GOX) and catalase (CAT), which either produce or consume H2O2, control the quantity of H2O2 in honey, which is why they are associated with the antibacterial and antioxidant properties of honey, and these enzymes play a crucial role in shielding the cell from reactive oxygen (ROS)-induced oxidative damage.55, 56 The results showed that isolate No 1 demonstrated the highest GOX activity (250.0 U/ml), followed by Mountain Honey (2337.5 U/ml), and the remainder of the isolates showed enzyme activity between 88 and 145 U/ml. Aspergillus niger and Penicillium glaucum are the known producers of GOX.57 Few studies have reported the production of GOX by bacteria,58 on contrary, several studies talk about GOX from honey.55 A recent study revealed that GOX is naturally produced by thermostable Streptomyces.58 Cruz et al59 confirm the importance of GOX in the food industry and reported that probiotic yogurts were produced with increased concentrations of GOX (0, 250, 500, 750, or 1,000 mg/kg).

Catalase was determined qualitatively, and honey and all the isolates showed remarkable activities with degrees of variation. On the contrary, Osés et al15 discovered that honey samples lacking catalase activity had extremely high peroxide values and that pollen had very high catalase activity while nectar had very little. Additionally, the results showed that the protease enzyme was totally absent in Mountain Honey and its isolates. Surprisingly, none of the bacterial isolates demonstrated protease activity, indicating a potential specificity in the enzymatic profile of honey-associated bacteria. This might be due to the absence of the protease gene in the mountain honey and, consequently, their isolation. The recently identified honey proteases may affect the quality and characteristics of honey.2

Microbial biofilms have always posed a serious risk to human health as well as the environment and the natural world. A long time ago, honey was mentioned as a strong antimicrobial agent.60 The presence of inactive antibiotic components in honey is responsible for its antibacterial properties. These include the pH's acidity, the osmotic action of carbohydrates, and peroxidase's generation of H2O2. Non-peroxidase compounds such as lysozyme, phenolic acids, and flavonoids have antibacterial action as well.60 This study aimed to establish a relationship between Nigerian mountain honey and its isolated bacteria through a comparison of the antibacterial activities of honey with various honey isolates. The results showed that the Nigerian mountain honey had a promising antimicrobial activity against all the tested pathogenic bacteria. According to Russell,60 Nigerian mountain honey possesses a greater degree of antibacterial activity that cannot be solely attributed to its osmolality, pH, and glucose oxidase activity. Hereafter, the term “non-peroxide active substance” or “UMF” refers to a substance that contributes to this activity. Also, the result revealed that the seven honey isolates had noticeable antimicrobial activity against Candida albicans. A recent study evaluated the effects of various honeys on Candida tropicalis biofilms, highlighting honey's potential as an effective antifungal agent.61 On the other hand, Abdel Wahab et al62 mentioned B endophyticus SH and Bacillus subtilis WA, as well as B endophyticus SH and Bacillus subtilis MO, as effective agents against Candida albicans ATCC 10231 and Candida tropicalis ATCC 13803, respectively. Honey and isolates NO. 1, 2, 5, 6, and 7 had antimicrobial activity against Salmonella enterica Typhi. Also, the isolates had antimicrobial activity against Staphylococcus aureus except isolates NO. 2 and 6 while, isolate NO.7 showed the highest activity (4.8 cm). This result refers to the validity of this isolate as a strong antimicrobial agent. Also, Nigerian mountain honey and its isolates recorded promising antimicrobial activity against Escherichia coli, except isolates No 4, 6, and 7. It was reported that bees’ honey showed antibacterial properties and therapeutic value against Salmonella typhimurium and Escherichia coli O157:H7 infections.

The excellent antibacterial activity of honey against clinical bacterial isolates indicated the usefulness of honey in clinical practice against bacterial infection This result means that not only honey is responsible for the alteration of the gut microbiome.63 Our results suggested that the benefit of honey resulted from a synergistic effect of honey and their isolates, as they play a role in creating a balance between pathogenic and beneficial microbial populations in the gut microbiome. This suggestion was confirmed by Hamdy et al5 and Abdelsamed et al,6 as they recommended honey as a new source for the probiotic bacteria.

The antimicrobial activity combined with the antioxidant properties of honey and its isolates has yet to be extensively and scientifically studied over a long period of time. Antioxidants are substances that prevent damage from being done by oxidants, which include lipid peroxyl radicals, O2, OH, superoxide, and/or other oxidants. Within this context, the antioxidant activity of the Nigerian mountain honey and its seven bacterial isolates was determined. The result reported that honey and its isolates showed high antioxidant activities ranging from 57 % to 87 %. Studies have indicated that honey originating from various floral sources and countries has noteworthy antioxidant properties The antioxidant activity of the bacterial honey isolates was supported by Abdelsamed et al,6 Esawy et al,4 Hamdy et al.5 Additionally, data suggests that honey and its isolates may be unique antioxidants that help prevent many diseases that are either directly or indirectly related to oxidative stress. Honey helps to prevent several acute and long-term illnesses, including cancer, diabetes, thrombotic, inflammatory, and allergy diseases.64 The most difficult aspect of cancer treatment was the chemotherapy toxic to healthy cells.65 Accordingly, the cytotoxicity of the seven levans extracted from bacterial-fermented medium and the honey was done against the normal human epithelial cell line (A431) Lev 1, Lev 2, and Nigerian mountain honey were selected to evaluate their anticancer activities against the human tumor cell line (s): HCT116 (Colon cell line) and A431 (skin cancer). The results showed that all the tested samples had an anticancer effect on HCT116 and a negative effect on A431. The recorded values for cell inhibition were 61.5, 59.5, and 53.70 % for honey, Lev 1, and Lev 2, respectively. Honey and its several components, like flavonoids and phenolics, are reported to inhibit the cell cycle of colon cancer cell lines in the G0/G1 phase.66 This inhibitory effect on tumor cell proliferation follows the downregulation of many cellular pathways via proteins such as tyrosine, cyclooxygenase, ornithine decarboxylase, and kinase. Thus, it can be hypothesized that honey or its components mediates inhibition of cell growth and is due to perturbation in the cell cycle, which may possibly lead to apoptosis.66 According to numerous reports, levan has anticancer effects against pancreatic cancer cell lines (MIA PaCa-2) and breast cancer cell lines (MCF-7 cells).67, 19 On the other hand, Abdel Wahab et al68 reported in coculture levan recorded 70.70 % inhibition against the hepatoblastoma cell line (HepG2) at 1000 µg/mL. While all three samples (5, 6, and 7) had cytotoxic effects on normal skin fibroblasts (BJ1). According to studies conducted by Abdel-Fattah et al,20 levan may have selective anticancer effects on hepatocellular carcinoma cells Levan polysaccharide has also been shown to enhance the anticancer and pro-apoptotic effects of breast cancer cells by causing reactive oxygen species (ROS) to be produced.69

The hydrolysis product of the polysaccharides of the seven bacterial isolates was identified by thin-layer chromatography (TLC). The results revealed that fructose was the main constituent of all the polymers with traces of glucose, and lev1 and lev2 comprise only fructose. The previous result indicated that the produced polysaccharides are levan polymers. Since levans can interact and affect the immune system, they are essential for treating a wide range of illnesses in humans.70, 71

The structure and functional group analysis of the two types of purified polymers were identified by the FTIR. The results for the two samples showed a wide spectrum peak of O–H stretching at 3259.41 cm−1 and 3270.72 cm−1 for Lev 1 and Lev 2, respectively. The broad-spectrum region is referred to as the massive OH group, which is a distinct characterization of the polysaccharides. The existence of stretching peaks present at 2933.46 cm−1 (Lev 1) and 2930.03 cm−1 (Lev 2) pointed to the methyl group and C–H stretching vibrations. There is distinct peak absorption at 1642.42 cm−1 and 1643.83 cm−1, which is due to the bound water.72 The band at 1461.61 cm−1 corresponds to the C

The regions at 1023.93 cm−1 and 1046.46 cm−1 are considered the fingerprints of the polysaccharides.69 The peaks around the signals 1133.16 cm−1, 988.56 cm−1, and 1101.84 cm−1, 1023.93 cm−1 were assigned to the stretching frequencies of C-O-C and C-O bonds, respectively, which might be attributed to the pyranose configuration of the sugar residue.72

The 1H and 13C NMR data highlight the complex and heterogeneous character of the EPS from Bacillus subtilis. The 13C NMR spectrum showed six intense resonances where the signal of the residue was detected at t δ61.0550, 104.5116, 74.8474, 77.6517, 82.9836, 62.6384, and 104.6642, 61.3172, 75.3148, 77.1080, 800, and 63.5350, which assigned C1-C6 for Lev 1 and Lev 2, respectively (Fig. 8a,c). This region reflected the presence of monosaccharide residues in Lev1 and Lev2, where it is a signature to distinguish the polysaccharides.72

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This investigation is a new attempt to compare the bioactivity of honey and their bacterial isolates. The results showed that there is a synergistic association between the honey and their microbiota. Also, the study suggested that the health benefit of consuming honey spoons is not only attributable to the honey alone but to the different bioactivities of their microbiota, which play a vital role in human health. The results suggest a potential interaction between honey and its associated microbiota, which may contribute to its biological properties; however, further studies with larger sample sizes are needed to confirm this observation. Additionally, it was found that the bacterial honey isolates were a new source of potential enzymes such as invertase, amylase, catalase, glucose oxidase, and levansucrase. The significance of bacterial honey isolates as possible sources of antioxidants and antimicrobials was also highlighted by the study. Furthermore, the isolated bacterial honey is a good source of significant polysaccharides, such as levan polymer.
